articles.full_text:
ANI
                
12 Oct 2026, 09:01 GMT+10
            
Singapore, October 12 (ANI): Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman held meetings with senior executives of five global financial institutions and investment firms in Singapore to discuss expanding their engagement in India across infrastructure financing, private credit, artificial intelligence (AI), renewable energy and housing finance.
According to posts shared by the Ministry of Finance on X, the meetings involved representatives from Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC), Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken (SEB), HPS Investment Partners, B Capital Group and Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG).
During her meeting with HPS Investment Partners CEO Scott Kapnick, Sitharaman discussed "private credit, structured finance and long-term financing for businesses".
The ministry's post said she encouraged HPS to explore setting up a fund in GIFT IFSC and collaboration with the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) to "mobilise financing for large infrastructure projects in India".
"HPS highlighted the potential to leverage debt capital to complement equity investments," the ministry said.
In talks with MUFG Chief Executive for Asia Pacific Yukinobu Saeki, discussions focused on expanding the bank's presence in India, particularly in "capital markets, infrastructure and project finance, renewable energy and M&A financing".
Sitharaman also encouraged greater engagement with the National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development (NaBFID) to support infrastructure financing. The meeting covered financing support for Indian small and medium enterprises and regulatory roadshows to "enhance market transparency and governance".
During her meeting with SEB Chairperson Marcus Wallenberg, discussions covered India's economic outlook and ways to strengthen investment flows from European institutional investors. The SEB team highlighted opportunities across "energy and data centres, IT and tax services, healthcare, financial services and housing finance".
The talks also covered sustainable finance, private equity investments in non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), the green transition and skill development.
Sitharaman also met SMBC Managing Executive Officer and Co-Head for Asia Pacific Rajeev Kannan to discuss opportunities to expand the bank's engagement in India, including "affordable housing finance, financing for NBFCs, trade finance and other priority sectors".
She encouraged the bank to explore investment and financing opportunities through NIIF and GIFT IFSC, particularly in aircraft leasing.
Separately, discussions with B Capital Group Co-founder and CEO Raj Ganguly focused on "Sovereign AI and the broader AI ecosystem". Sitharaman highlighted India's potential to emerge as a leader in AI services and encouraged the firm to explore AI applications in banking and financial services.
The ministry said B Capital emphasised the importance of a "stable currency and predictable, transparent tax policies" for investors.
The discussions covered potential avenues to expand financing for Indian businesses and infrastructure and attract investment across technology, energy and other sectors. (ANI)

articles.title: Vietnam’s electronics import surge reflects AI demand, production expansion - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Vietnam’s electronics import surge reflects AI demand, production expansion  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Vietnam’s merchandise imports rose 36.7% in the first nine months of 2026, significantly outpacing export growth as electronics companies increased component inventories and expanded production capacity.
The sharp rise in imports reflects the combined impact of investment cycles, input prices and Vietnam’s growing role in global electronics supply chains, including products related to artificial intelligence.
AI boom drives imports
Vietnam’s merchandise imports reached $453.72 billion in the nine-month period, up 36.7% from a year earlier, according to the National Statistics Office. Exports totalled $434.30 billion, a year-on-year increase of 24.5%, bringing total trade to $888.02 billion, up 30.4%.
The country recorded a merchandise trade deficit of $19.42 billion over the nine-month period, although it posted a surplus of $1.27 billion in September alone.
Foreign-invested enterprises generated $350.41 billion in exports, up 29.4% year-on-year and accounting for 80.7% of the national total. By contrast, exports by domestic companies reached $83.89 billion, rising just 7.5%. The figures indicate that export growth remains heavily concentrated in the foreign-invested sector.
On the import side, foreign-invested firms recorded $335.55 billion, up 42% year-on-year, while domestic businesses imported $118.17 billion, an increase of 23.5%. The gap in growth rates suggests that import demand among foreign-invested businesses, which make up a large share of electronics and high-tech manufacturing, is expanding faster than that of domestic enterprises.
According to the Ministry of Industry and Trade (MoIT), machinery, equipment, raw materials and fuels used in domestic production and export processing account for around 90.5% of total imports.
Pham Van Quan, deputy director of the ministry’s Industry Agency, said the trend should also be viewed in a positive light. He said additional equipment imports could reflect efforts to expand production lines, prepare manufacturing capacity, and meet peak consumer demand at the end of the year.
Investors have assessed Vietnam’s reforms by merging localities, ministries and agencies, improving institutions and cutting administrative procedures, as moving in a positive direction, Quan said.
As a result, they have confidently scaled up production, importing additional equipment and expanding production lines in preparation for the peak consumption season in the fourth quarter. This is a peak period for manufacturing businesses, he added.
Trinh Thu Hien, deputy director of the ministry’s Agency of Foreign Trade, identified three main factors behind the increase in imports, particularly in the electronics and semiconductor sectors.
The first is rising global raw material prices. She said prices of some chips and solid-state drives (SSDs) had increased by 300% to 500%. As a result, even if import volumes remained at the previous year’s level, the value of imports could still rise sharply because of higher prices.
Second, electronics companies are increasing inventories and stockpiling raw materials to meet demand for AI-related products. Some materials have become scarce, with supply shortages occurring at times, prompting certain factories and companies to extend inventory coverage from around six weeks to 12 weeks. Meanwhile, the inventory value of some businesses has risen from $100 million to $700 million.
The third factor is production expansion by electronics and semiconductor companies. Hien cited Samsung’s increased investment in Thai Nguyen province, Intel’s relocation of a factory from Costa Rica to Vietnam, and BYD’s expansion and upgrading of its investment in Phu Tho province.
Vietnam benefits from AI supply chains, but domestic value added remains limited
The World Bank Group’s October 2026 East Asia and Pacific Economic Update said the wave of high-tech manufacturing and exports serving AI demand is supporting growth in several economies participating in global supply chains.
The WB raised its forecast for Vietnam’s GDP growth in 2026 by 1.1 percentage points from its previous projection to 7.4%. This was the largest upward revision among economies in Asia and the Pacific.
According to the report, in the 12 months ending in April 2026, six economies - China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam - exported a combined $1.4 trillion worth of AI-related goods. Over the same period, the U.S. imported around $739 billion worth of these products, with approximately one-third originating in East Asia and the Pacific.
Vietnam’s exports of AI-related goods have more than doubled compared with the 2020-2022 average. The country primarily participates in downstream equipment assembly, with computers, servers and routers accounting for around 60% of its AI-related goods exports. A significant share of these exports serves final demand in the U.S.
However, export growth has been accompanied by substantial import demand. According to the WB, Vietnam’s imports grew faster than exports in 2026, partly because companies increased their inventories of electronics, semiconductor prices rose and fuel costs remained high.
This indicates that Vietnam’s technology manufacturing and exports remain closely linked to overseas supplies of components and raw materials.
Alongside the growth opportunities, the WB also highlighted risks if expectations for AI’s economic returns are not met, potentially triggering financial market adjustments and affecting investment.
Franziska Ohnsorge, WB chief economist for Asia, said Vietnam is deeply integrated into AI-related supply chains. If the trend of strong AI demand continues, Vietnam will have significant opportunities to benefit and sustain high growth. However, this is also a risk factor because if the AI trend reverses, Vietnam’s growth could be affected.
Despite strong growth in electronics trade, domestic value added remains limited. According to the government’s assessment in Notice No. 481/TB-VPCP dated September 14, 2026, Vietnam’s electronics industry remains heavily dependent on imported components, raw materials and technology, while domestic companies have limited participation in supply chains.
Following a meeting last month with the Vietnam Electronic Industries Association and several major electronics and semiconductor import-export companies, Standing Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc instructed the Ministry of Industry and Trade to work with businesses reporting large gaps between import and export turnover, particularly those with substantial trade deficits. The aim is to clarify the structure and purpose of their imports and the extent to which these imports support production and exports.
The ministry was also tasked with reviewing the list of priority supporting-industry products for the electronics sector, focusing on components and materials with strong demand and potential for domestic production.
Another task is to develop a program to connect and develop Vietnamese suppliers for domestic and foreign electronics, semiconductor and technology firms, based on individual product supply chains, technical standards and business requirements.
At the same time, the government has called for stronger links between foreign-invested enterprises and domestic businesses, alongside support to help Vietnamese companies improve technological capabilities and quality management and participate in higher-value-added, technology-intensive stages of production.
At the MoIT’s regular press briefing, Hien, deputy director of the Agency of Foreign Trade, said the ministry’s measures focused on improving institutional and policy frameworks, developing markets and supporting businesses. In the longer term, the goal is to strengthen the capabilities of Vietnamese enterprises and increase the domestic value added of products manufactured in Vietnam.

articles.title: My Say: The SME crisis: How China’s exported over-capacity is gutting Malaysia’s private sector - KLSE Screener
articles.summary: My Say: The SME crisis: How China’s exported over-capacity is gutting Malaysia’s private sector  KLSE Screener
articles.full_text:
This article first appeared in Forum, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on October 12, 2026 - October 18, 2026
Our small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are in real danger of being gutted by their hyper-competitive counterparts from China whose overcapacity is being exported to our domestic markets. They create very little domestic employment and value-add, bringing in an en bloc shipment of labour and overheads, materials and supply chain that are wholly unregulated and untaxed from China.
Malaysia’s private sector-driven SME ecosystem has almost none of the protectionist character of the monopolies and oligopolies that dominate the government-linked company (GLC)/government-linked investment company (GLIC) ecosystem. Our SMEs have to operate under strict financial discipline with limited funding liquidity, while navigating a high level of regulatory demands on their operations and high costs.
Retail units, mechanics’ workshops, construction services and supply chains, food and beverage (F&B) outlets and other service-oriented businesses are not abstract numbers on an economist’s spreadsheet. These are real enterprises that have survived for years, employed people, paid taxes and supported families and funded education for the next generation. The Chinese onslaught has already started to decimate this sector one by one. Once gone, they will never return, together with the employment of our people.
When people across such different sectors start telling the same story at the same time — margins disappearing, customers slowing down, costs rising, price competition becoming impossible and businesses simply trying to survive — we should not dismiss them as isolated business failures or a lack of ability to compete. Maybe the official macro numbers haven’t captured these yet. Maybe nobody has properly measured these or has raised the alarm. But these signals are real. By the time everyone agrees there is a crisis, a lot of these businesses will already be gone for good. Many retailers have already made it known that they will be closing shop after Chinese New Year.
We need to understand the systemic issues that the global phenomenon of China’s dominance is creating and take the necessary steps, or we shall probably see the beginning of the end for our generations-old SME sector, which is the largest tax-paying segment and the backbone of our economy.
China’s capital misallocation and the resultant exported surplus
So, let us understand why this is happening. China’s macroeconomic model today faces a persistent structural imbalance. High domestic savings rates and state-directed financial intervention have systemically prioritised industrial capacity over private consumption. China’s gross national savings rate sits at about 43% to 45% of gross domestic product (GDP), roughly double the global average.
A glaring structural problem compounds this issue: real estate historically represented 60% to 70% of Chinese household wealth. That bubble has burst, led by Evergrande and Country Garden, which together accumulated roughly US$500 billion (RM2.04 trillion) in liabilities. This problem does not seem to be going away anytime soon and the result has exacerbated several underlying issues:
● Weak consumer base: Despite generating about 30% of global manufacturing output, China’s domestic consumption remains weak.
● Capital redirection: As internal real estate investment contracts, state-backed capital has been redirected to industrial manufacturing output.
● Exporting surplus: Lacking domestic absorption capacity, state-subsidised excess production across heavy industrial goods, solar photovoltaic modules and consumer retail products are routed outwards. Today, this export push extends to the services sector.
● Growth mandates: The Chinese Communist Party’s political narrative relies heavily on economic output. GDP growth targets remain a critical key performance indicator for provincial officials.
● Scale disparity: China operates with an active workforce of 725 million people in provincial production clusters developing a hyper-competitive supply chain within these clusters. No nation on earth can match this scale or build such tightly integrated domestic supply chains.
● Provincial scale: Eleven Chinese provinces maintain working populations exceeding 30 million each — from Guangxi at around 30 million to Guangdong at around 70 million — competing fiercely in overlapping product categories.
● Global context: By comparison, the active labour forces of the European Union, the US and Brazil stand at roughly 195 million, 168 million and 108 million respectively. Malaysia’s total workforce stands at a modest 17.3 million. In short, in terms of industrial scale, there is absolutely no contest.
● Wage arbitrage realities: National Bureau of Statistics figures show that China’s urban private sector median monthly wage sits at roughly RMB4,500 (RM2,745) to RMB4,800, while its baseline rural migrant workforce averages RMB5,075. By comparison, Department of Statistics Malaysia figures place Malaysia’s formal sector median monthly wage at RM3,065. This indicates that the country’s baseline labour cost sits functionally on par with China’s, leaving Malaysian SMEs unable to rely on wage cost advantages to offset China’s massive industrial scale and state-backed capital efficiencies and subsidies.
● Urban unemployment mechanics: China’s surveyed urban unemployment rate hovers between 4.8% and 5.3%. Taking just the urban employed population of 470 million, a 5% unemployment rate represents roughly 23.5 million unemployed urban workers (excluding youth unemployment). When their unemployment number dwarfs our total workforce, and their gargantuan employed workforce has a median wage equal to or less than our own, even the most efficient businesses cannot compete with such scale.
Put together, this structural dynamic enables an unprecedented wave of global export dominance without military power, presenting an insurmountable challenge for smaller economies. Unregulated cross-border services and trade flows ensure that local providers are inevitably priced out of their own domestic market.
Global and domestic impact on Malaysian SMEs
For Malaysian SMEs, competing against this influx of capital and workforce is not merely an issue of operational efficiency. It is a matter of financial reality. Local private enterprises operate under commercial discipline, bearing standard market-rate borrowing terms and statutory tax obligations. They cannot absorb a prolonged margin squeeze against foreign entities operating under sovereign liquidity mandates that prioritise global market share over return on invested capital. They do not have the scale or almost monopolistic size to force supply chain vendors to provide practically zero-interest financing the way BYD Co, for example, does for its contractors with nearly nine-month payment terms.
This is systemic unfair trade competition that no efficiency improvement or tariffs can ever redress. I am sounding the alarm because while our consumers may enjoy lower costs now, after decades of our own economic misallocation and leakages of capital, especially within our GLIC and GLC economy, the impact will be felt when domestic SMEs disappear, and wages will be further compressed or ultimately dry up altogether along with our SMEs.
The steel sector: Enclave capital and overcapacity
The first primary industrial casualty of this dynamic we have witnessed has been Malaysia’s iron and steel sector. Malaysian Iron and Steel Industry Federation (Misif) data indicates national apparent steel consumption between 7.5 million and 9.5 million tonnes annually. However, total domestic capacity has expanded sharply past 24 million tonnes, driven primarily by mega-scale foreign investment projects.
The establishment of integrated steel complexes in the Malaysia-China Kuantan Industrial Park (MCKIP) — such as Alliance Steel (M) Sdn Bhd — introduced immense capacity into a saturated regional market:
● Capacity utilisation failure: Domestic long-steel capacity utilisation rates dropped below 50%, well beneath the 70% to 80% threshold required for cash break-even operations.
● Upstream displacements: Incumbent domestic producers such as Kinsteel Bhd and Perwaja Steel Sdn Bhd faced severe balance sheet distress, forced restructurings or liquidation. Local re-rollers operating without sovereign debt backstops could not survive below-cost market pricing.
● Enclave operations: Rather than integrating with local supply chains, these major foreign-backed industrial enclaves from China mainly import machinery, technical services and feedstock directly, minimising if not eliminating local procurement altogether. Unlike previous investment models, here multipliers and domestic wage spillovers are absent.
Across fellow Asean and BRICS economies, notably Brazil, Indonesia and Vietnam, governments have enacted anti-dumping duties and introduced strict local content mandates to preserve domestic manufacturing ecosystems. Ours provide attractive land deals and unneeded incentives, when we are already a stable political investment destination at the expense of our own domestic economy and employment.
Digital micro-retail and de minimis arbitrage
This onslaught has extended from heavy industry to light manufacturing, wholesale distribution and commercial services. The expansion of ultra-low-cost direct-from-factory e-commerce platforms bypasses traditional domestic retail networks.
While Malaysia introduced a 10% low value goods sales tax on imported goods priced below RM500, cross-border sellers continued to exploit customs tariff structures and direct-shipping subsidies. Local bricks-and-mortar retailers — bearing commercial property leases, regulatory compliance costs and standard import tariffs on bulk stock — face a structural cost disadvantage. Concurrently, China’s businesses bring with them huge cash reserves to snap up commercial real estate

articles.title: Imports and exports are heading towards the $1.2 trillion mark. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Imports and exports are heading towards the $1.2 trillion mark.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:

| Electronics continues to be one of the main drivers of export growth. | 
 Imports and exports in the first nine months increased by more than $207 billion.
 Nearly $118 billion was the total value of imports and exports in September, marking a new record for foreign trade activity.
Vietnam.
 This result far surpasses the approximately $110 billion mark achieved in July and August. Compared to the same period in 2015, total import and export turnover in September increased by 42.4%.
 The surge in international trade in September contributed to the total import and export turnover for the first nine months of this year reaching $888 billion, a 30.4% increase compared to the same period last year, and also the highest nine-month figure ever recorded. 
 Vietnam, import and export, import and export 2026, import and export turnover, US$1.2 trillion, international trade, foreign trade, exports, imports, trade balance, trade deficit, trade surplus, FDI, domestic enterprises, electronics, computers, telephones, machinery and equipment  The 30.4% increase corresponds to over $207 billion in absolute value.
 Vietnam's import and export activities in the first nine months of 2026 continued to maintain high growth momentum, becoming one of the important drivers of economic growth.
 After nine months, total exports reached $434.3 billion, an increase of 24.5%, equivalent to an increase of approximately $85.4 billion; imports reached $453.72 billion, an increase of 36.7%, equivalent to an increase of approximately $121.8 billion compared to the same period last year.
 However, along with the high export growth since the beginning of the year, imports have increased even more sharply, mainly in the group of machinery, equipment, and input materials for production and export. Therefore, the trade balance shifted to a trade deficit right from the beginning of the year.
 A positive sign for goods trade in September was the reversal of the trade balance, with a surplus of $1.27 billion after several months of deficits. As a result, the cumulative trade deficit decreased from $20.46 billion after eight months to $19.42 billion after nine months.
 The scale of trade has expanded.
 Tracking import and export figures month by month this year reveals a very rapid expansion in trade volume.
 While total trade turnover in the first month of the year only reached $88.16 billion, subsequent months saw strong growth, except for February, which experienced a drop to $67.16 billion due to the extended Lunar New Year holiday. By May, turnover had exceeded $99 billion, and from June 2026 onwards, it surpassed $100 billion for the first time.
 The following two months saw the figure consistently hover around $110 billion, before surging to nearly $118 billion in September.
 These developments indicate increasingly vibrant trade and the formation of a new benchmark for Vietnam's international trade turnover in 2026.
 Not only has the volume of imports and exports increased, but they have also diversified, especially in the industrial, electronic, machinery, input material, and product categories that are deeply involved in global supply chains.
 Most impressively, the electronics sector saw production, exports, and imports all increase far beyond forecasts. According to statistics, in September alone, the entire electronics industry achieved export turnover of $28.73 billion, of which the electronics and computer group reached $22.56 billion, an increase of 112.7% compared to September 2025; and telephones reached $6.17 billion, an increase of 14.3%.
 By the end of September 2026, exports from this sector totaled $175.4 billion. Of this, computers and electronics accounted for $123.6 billion, an increase of 59.6%; and telephones accounted for $51.7 billion, an increase of 18.8% compared to the same period last year.
 Total electronics imports in the first nine months reached approximately $197 billion. Thus, total electronics exports and imports after nine months exceeded $372 billion, accounting for about 42% of the country's total exports and imports. 
 Concerns remain about the quality of growth.
 Production and trade activities in the first nine months maintained a positive trend, but some structural risks also emerged that need to be proactively managed in the remaining months of the year.
 At the conference summarizing the tasks for the third quarter (September 2026) and outlining the tasks for October and the direction for the fourth quarter of 2026 of the Ministry of Industry and Trade, the issue of growth quality was once again mentioned.
 “Imports and the trade balance continue to reflect both positive aspects and structural risks. Imports have increased much more sharply than exports; the trade balance shows a large trade deficit. Approximately 90.5% of imports are machinery and raw materials for production, but the concentration of supply sources remains high,” said Mr. Bui Huy Son, Director of the Planning and Finance Department ( Ministry of Industry and Trade ).
 More notably, while exports increased sharply by 24.5%, continuing to be a prominent driving force, the quality of growth is uneven, and the gap in contribution between the two business sectors continues to widen.
 The FDI sector accounted for 80.7% of total export turnover and increased by 29.4%, contributing $350.41 billion, while the domestic enterprise sector only increased by 7.5%, reaching $83.89 billion, accounting for 19.3% of total export turnover.
 This is clearly demonstrated in the three main export product groups: computers, telephones and components, machinery, equipment and spare parts, with a total turnover of over $230 billion after 9 months, but the majority belongs to the FDI sector.
 Conversely, textiles and footwear – sectors with a greater participation of domestic businesses – are facing slowing growth. After nine months, textiles generated $30.3 billion, an increase of only 1.9%; footwear reached $18 billion, an increase of 1.4% compared to the same period last year.
 The quality of growth is also clearly reflected in the trade balance. While the domestic economic sector had a trade deficit of $34.28 billion, the FDI sector, including crude oil, had a trade surplus of $14.86 billion.
 Assessing trade outlook for Q4
 In the final months of the year, import and export activities are expected to remain vibrant thanks to the start of the peak consumer season. This will strongly support international production and trade.
 Nevertheless, the trade imbalance may persist.
 The General Statistics Office predicts that imports are likely to continue increasing faster than exports due to the continued high demand for machinery, equipment, electronic components, raw materials, energy, and auxiliary materials serving export industries at the end of the year. Furthermore, trade imbalances in some markets also expose exports to greater risks from trade protection measures.
 Currently, Vietnam has a trade surplus with the US of $122.62 billion, an increase of 23.8% compared to the same period last year; a trade surplus with the EU of $36.06 billion, an increase of 25.3%; and a trade surplus with Japan of $2.65 billion, an increase of 85.9%.
 Minister of Industry and Trade Le Manh Hung acknowledged that, in the remaining months of this year, commodity trade will continue to face pressure from external factors such as unpredictable fluctuations in global trade, inflation, and climate change.
 He requested that functional units within the Ministry proactively identify, forecast, and develop appropriate response solutions for the remaining months of the year. The spirit is to build a set of operational solutions for the fourth quarter based on the available space and growth drivers.
 Regarding the trade balance, following the return of a trade surplus in September, the Minister set a target for the remainder of the year to reduce the trade deficit to below $10 billion. Accordingly, it is necessary to effectively utilize the signed FTAs; manage foreign markets according to a long-term strategy, and expand opportunities in potential markets. Simultaneously, focus should be placed on trade defense, strengthening early warning systems, sharing information, and connecting with localities to address issues related to trade investigations.
 According to calculations, after 9 months, total import and export turnover reached 888 billion USD. To reach the 1,200 billion USD mark, the fourth quarter needs to achieve an additional approximately 312 billion USD, equivalent to an average of about 104 billion USD per month - lower than the average turnover of the third quarter.
 Meanwhile, import and export turnover tends to increase in the last months of the year due to increased production and consumption demand. This is an important area for the total turnover for the whole year 2026 to aim for, or even surpass, the $1.2 trillion mark.
 The General Statistics Office believes that, considering the scale of trade turnover already achieved, the $1.2 trillion mark is achievable and entirely feasible if import and export activities maintain their current growth rate in the remaining months of the year.

On the morning of Oct 9, thick white smog blanketed the old town, obscuring the sea facing Indonesia’s Sumatra island across the Strait of Malacca. The 80-year-old was left cutting honeydew slices in his stall, with a few people in sight, including a handful of breakfast goers at a nearby food court.
“It’s a holiday today, I know there’s some haze, but why are the kids not out to play?” he told The Straits Times.

Johor has since extended its shutdown until Oct 16.
The federal government on Oct 8 extended closures to Melaka, Negeri Sembilan, Selangor, Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya and Rompin district in Pahang. Schools in Melaka, parts of Perak and Kuala Lumpur are set to reopen on Oct 12 as air quality improves.
Pasir Gudang, about 20km from Johor Bahru and across the Tebrau Strait from Singapore, repeatedly recorded some of Malaysia’s highest API readings in recent days. At 5pm on Oct 9, it recorded the highest nationwide API reading at the time of 190.
Sarawak declared an emergency in Serian district on Sept 4 when it recorded an API reading of 521, but the air quality across the state is currently in the “moderate” category.
The haze has been linked by some to a tragedy in Pontian district in Johor. On Oct 8, three siblings were killed when their motorcycle collided with a lorry on a rural road. Social media users blamed it on poor visibility due to the haze, even as the cause of the accident is still under police investigation.
“I saw news of the accident… even when I was driving here, the visibility was really bad and things can get dangerous with the haze,” said Iskandar Samsudin, 34, a wiring contractor from Pasir Gudang, who was at the Pontian seaside park on Oct 9 with his three children.
“I’m concerned too, about my health, my children’s health and my safety,” he added.
Across Johor, residents and businesses reported weaker sales.
Khaleeda Mohd Khuzzan, 27, who owns a cafe in Batu Pahat, said lunch crowds remained steady but evening business had declined over the past week.
Oil palm farmer Ahmad Zamri Daris, 46, from Parit Raja in Batu Pahat, said some of his family members are experiencing symptoms like coughing. Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is the main pollutant of concern. These particles can be deposited within the lower airways and lungs, causing irritation.
On a more positive note, lawyer Alias Rasman said conditions in Kota Tinggi, on the eastern side of Johor near Desaru, were clearer than at his Johor Bahru office.
Night markets continued to operate in Johor Bahru and Iskandar Puteri, but vendors said crowds have thinned.
At a night market in Eco Botanic in Iskandar Puteri on Oct 10, sales assistant Lim Wei Yang said he had sold just 20 packets of laundry capsules by 9.30pm, after starting work at noon. This is just half of the amount he usually sells in a day.
In Johor Bahru’s popular central square, Sri Gelam, crowds – mostly families – were still seen at the public playground and field, but members of running clubs that usually train there at night were absent.
In Iskandar Puteri, football proved to be a bigger draw. Johor Darul Ta’zim (JDT), the state’s national champion club, drew 15,000 and 13,000 fans to home matches at Sultan Ibrahim Stadium on Oct 8 and 9 – which the club specifically scheduled – respectively.
At all these locations, it was rare to see people wearing masks.
“My eyes do feel a bit irritated and the air smells of thick charred chocolate or cocoa powder,” said Hizan Abdullah, 60, who attended the club’s ASEAN Club Championship match against Cambodia’s PKR Svay Rieng FC on Oct 8.
While sales have taken a hit, the matches were a silver lining for roving drinks seller Khairil Azwan, 45, who was at the JDT game on Oct 8.
“Johor is unusually quiet these few days and it’s really weird,” he said, noting that sales had dropped 40 per cent the past few days.
Experts told ST that relief from the haze might not come until December, as an El Nino event was contributing to hotter, drier conditions prolonging the haze situation.
Citing data from the ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre, Forestry researcher and University of Nottingham Malaysia adjunct professor Teckwyn Lim said: “The western side of the Malaysian peninsula, such as in Johor and in the Klang Valley, is more affected by the haze because they are closer to Sumatra.”
Meanwhile, Malaysia’s King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar has urged schools in affected areas to close if API readings remained between unhealthy levels of 150 and 180 for prolonged periods. He also advised the public to wear masks and limit outdoor activities.
Johor Menteri Besar Onn Hafiz Ghazi on Oct 7 called on ASEAN to convene an emergency meeting to address the transboundary haze.
“Our approach here is not to point fingers at any party, but rather to find a collective solution,” he said.
Correction note: In an earlier version of the story, we wrote that the football game was at Sultan Ismail Stadium. This is incorrect. It should be Sultan Ibrahim Stadium. We are sorry for the error.

articles.title: Navigating the future, together: Singapore-Philippines economic ties - The Manila Times
articles.summary: Navigating the future, together: Singapore-Philippines economic ties  The Manila Times
articles.full_text:
THE Philippines’ attainment of upper-middle-income status is an important milestone in its economic development. This achievement has also opened up new possibilities for the country and its partners, including Singapore.
For Singapore, economic progress is always about moving forward together with our friends and partners. As a small country with limited natural resources and a small domestic market, we have had to remain open to the world, invest in our people and build strong relationships. These principles continue to guide us as we navigate an increasingly uncertain global economy.
Singapore’s economy grew by 4.8% in 2025 and is projected to expand by 4.5% to 5.5% in 2026. The stronger-than-expected performance has been supported by manufacturing and services, particularly electronics, financial services and information and communications, as well as global demand related to artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced semiconductors.
But the external environment remains uncertain. Geopolitical tensions, trade disruptions and technological change are reshaping the global economy. For a country whose prosperity depends on international trade and investment, these developments have direct implications for our growth.
Our response is to strengthen our competitiveness while deepening our connections with the world. We are investing in emerging industries such as AI, advanced manufacturing and the green economy while helping our businesses and workers adapt to change. We are also expanding our economic linkages, recognising that our future prosperity is inextricably linked to the region and beyond.
This is where our longstanding partnership with the Philippines has particular significance.
We already have a strong foundation. Bilateral trade in goods between Singapore and the Philippines reached S$21.47 billion in 2025. Singapore was also the Philippines’ largest ASEAN export market that year, taking US$3.53 billion, or 29.9%, of Philippine exports to ASEAN. Singapore has consistently ranked among the Philippines’ leading sources of foreign investment, accounting for almost 34% of approved foreign investment pledges in 2025. This momentum has continued in 2026, with Philippine Statistics Authority data placing Singapore among the Philippines’ top three sources of approved foreign investment in both the first and second quarters of the year. Singapore companies are active in sectors ranging from digital infrastructure and telecommunications to aviation, logistics, healthcare and financial services.
But our economic relationship is more than trade and investment flows. Singapore’s connections to capital, technology and international markets complement the Philippines’ growing market, young workforce, strong services sector and considerable potential in areas like digitalisation and renewable energy. These complementary strengths allow businesses from both countries to grow together and reach new markets.
Technology is a good place to start. The Philippines’ digital economy was worth PHP2.74 trillion in 2025, equivalent to 9.8% of GDP, and employed more than 10 million people. Singapore’s technology ecosystem and the Philippines’ digital talent and tech-enabled services industry provide a strong basis
for enhanced collaboration. During President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr.’s visit to Singapore this July, our leaders agreed to deepen cooperation in AI, while Singapore businesses discussed further investments in data infrastructure and telecommunications.
The green economy is another area where our interests converge. Singapore is pursuing energy transition and developing capabilities in sustainable finance and carbon services, while the Philippines has substantial renewable-energy resources and energy needs. Our bilateral Implementation Agreement on Carbon Credits Cooperation, signed this April, provides a framework to mobilise climate finance for projects that support sustainable development and benefit local communities.
Our interests also extend beyond our bilateral relationship. ASEAN remains central to our economic future. In 2025, ASEAN was Singapore’s largest merchandise trading partner, with two-way trade reaching US$4,370 billion. Singapore’s foreign direct investment inflows into ASEAN rose from US$23.8 billion in 2024 to US$33.7 billion in 2025, underscoring our growing ties with the region. At a time when global trade faces greater uncertainty, doubling down on regional integration can help our businesses diversify markets, strengthen supply chains and seize new opportunities for growth.
The Philippines’ ASEAN Chairmanship in 2026 has helped advance this agenda. Under the Philippines’ leadership, ASEAN has made significant progress in strengthening regional economic integration. The upgraded ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement is expected to enter into force ahead of schedule, simplifying customs procedures and reducing the cost of trading across the region. The ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), which we hope to sign in November, will facilitate cross
border digital trade, payments, and services, giving businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises, greater access to the region. According to the ASEAN DEFA Study, successful implementation of DEFA could help ASEAN’s digital economy reach US$2 trillion by 2030. ASEAN has also begun laying the groundwork for a Green Economy Framework Agreement, which could support the development of an interoperable regional carbon market and attract investment into sustainable projects. Equally important is ASEAN’s continued engagement beyond the region. ASEAN is pursuing free trade talks with Korea, India and Canada while exploring the expansion of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership. These efforts will give our businesses access to new markets, diversify supply chains and reinforce ASEAN’s position as an attractive destination for investment.
Singapore looks forward to building on the Philippines’ achievements when we assume the ASEAN Chairmanship in 2027. We will work with fellow ASEAN Member States to further regional economic integration, strengthen ties and translate these agreements into tangible benefits for businesses and our people. It is in all our interests that ASEAN remains open, connected and competitive.
For Singapore and the Philippines, we have an opportunity to deepen our economic partnership, drawing on our complementary strengths in digitalisation, sustainable development and regional connectivity. By bringing together our businesses, expertise and networks, we can create more possibilities for our people and our youths, while contributing to ASEAN’s continued growth.

articles.title: FDI must be linked to market expansion and greening of production. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: FDI must be linked to market expansion and greening of production.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| Attracting FDI in the new phase focuses on quality, high technology, and increased linkages with domestic businesses. | 
 Large export volume but low level of self-reliance.
 "Entering a new phase of development, we should not focus on how much FDI we attract or how much exports increase, but rather on how much real value FDI has created and is creating for the economy ."
 Dr. Nguyen Nhu Quynh, Director of the National Institute for Economic and Financial Strategy and Policy (NIEF) under the Ministry of Finance, expressed this view when discussing the orientation for attracting FDI at the workshop "Improving legal policies on managing and attracting foreign investment in Vietnam in the new era," chaired by the Ministry of Public Security in coordination with the Ministry of Finance last weekend.
 Vietnam continues to be a positive destination for international capital flows. According to the General Statistics Office, as of September 30, 2026, the total registered FDI capital in Vietnam reached US$50.36 billion, an increase of 76.4% compared to the same period last year. 
 Vietnam still needs to attract a large amount of FDI to serve its development, but the quality must be higher. Policies need to shift from 'attracting more' to 'selecting the right investments,' ensuring rapid implementation, effective spillover effects, and reduced emissions. The projected FDI demand for the 2026-2030 period is approximately US$43.4 billion per year.  - Dr. Nguyen Nhu Quynh, Director of the National Institute for Economic and Financial Strategy and Policy (NIEF), 
Ministry of Finance  Realized FDI reached over $21 billion, an increase of 12.1% and the highest level in the past 5 years.
 Foreign direct investment (FDI) continues to favor Vietnam, but the current challenge is how to direct this capital into sectors that the economy needs, while simultaneously creating greater added value for domestic businesses.
 According to Dr. Nguyen Nhu Quynh, after more than 40 years of attracting FDI, this capital flow has contributed to expanding production capacity, boosting exports, and enabling Vietnam to participate more deeply in the global value chain.
 However, the level of dependence on the FDI sector is increasing. In 2015, exports from the FDI sector reached US$110.56 billion.
After 10 years, this figure increased to $368.8 billion, a 3.34-fold increase. Meanwhile, imports by the FDI sector also increased from $97.23 billion to $317.63 billion.
 By the end of September 2026, the FDI sector accounted for over 80% of the country's total export turnover, reaching US$350.41 billion. This sector also accounted for a large proportion of the export turnover of many key product groups: computers at 99.7%; telephones at 99%; and machinery and equipment at 94.4%.
 "Vietnam's leading position in manufacturing and exporting does not entirely equate to the capabilities of Vietnamese businesses. While export turnover is high, the value created within Vietnam is not commensurate," Mr. Quynh observed.
 According to experts attending the workshop, heavy reliance on FDI also poses certain risks. For example, Samsung accounts for a large share of Vietnam's electronics exports. When this corporation adjusts its product portfolio or reallocates production activities among countries, the impact could quickly spread to the supply chain in Vietnam, affecting exports and jobs.
 Therefore, attracting FDI in the coming period needs to be closely linked to commitments on expanding export markets, greening production chains, and developing domestic supply systems.
 Increase exports, reduce market risks.
 Statistical data shows that Vietnam's exports have increased sharply, but the level of market concentration remains high.
 The five major markets and market regions, including the US, China, the EU, South Korea , and Japan, currently account for approximately 70% of total export value.
 "Just a change in tariffs, technical adjustments, or standards in a large market like the US can make it difficult for domestic production and supply chains to 'respond'," expressed Dr. Nguyen Hoa Cuong, Deputy Director of the Institute for Policy and Strategy Research (Central Committee for Policy and Strategy).
 According to Mr. Cuong, Vietnam is leading ASEAN in the ratio of FDI to GDP. However, focusing solely on the scale of capital flows can easily lead to complacency with past achievements and the risk of falling into a "processing and assembly trap." This is because Vietnam ranks last among ASEAN-5 countries in terms of domestic added value in exports.
 In the context of import markets increasingly demanding higher technical standards and sustainable development requirements, FDI projects in Vietnam in the coming period need to meet these stringent requirements.
 Furthermore, FDI must create a ripple effect on the domestic business sector, helping Vietnamese businesses increase their localization rate and participate more deeply in supply chains, thereby facilitating technology transfer.
 Mr. Cuong emphasized that the role of the State also needs to be more clearly demonstrated in policy-making and supply chain management. Regulatory agencies need to be able to monitor and evaluate the operations of production chains in Vietnam, thereby promptly identifying risks and
There are appropriate policies.
 One positive sign is that Vietnam has recently attracted a number of FDI projects in the manufacturing sector that align with its green and sustainable development orientation.
 A prime example is the Lego Group's factory project in VSIP III Industrial Park, Binh Duong province (now part of Ho Chi Minh City), with an investment of $1 billion.
The factory will officially open in April 2025.
 According to Lego Group, at the time of its inauguration, Lego Manufacturing Vietnam was the group's most environmentally sustainable factory, aiming to operate on 100% renewable energy.
 This is one of the projects that shows the trend of attracting FDI is gradually shifting from prioritizing capital scale to focusing more on technology, the environment, and the sustainability of production activities.
 The level of commitment fulfilled will determine the level of incentives offered.
 Vietnam has now attracted investors from over 150 countries and territories. However, nearly 80% of FDI still comes from Asian economies such as China, Singapore , South Korea, and Hong Kong, while the proportion of capital from countries with strong technological capabilities remains relatively low.
 FDI flows continue to concentrate in localities with high growth rates and developed infrastructure, while many other localities still face difficulties in attracting investment.
 In this context, the approach to attracting FDI in the coming period needs a fundamental change. Resolution 10-NQ/TW, dated June 8, 2026, of the Politburo on the development of the foreign-invested economy has clearly defined the direction for selecting capital flows: prioritizing quality over quantity; limiting labor-intensive and processing projects; prioritizing high technology, green transformation, and closely linking economic development with national security.
 According to Ms. Bui Thu Thuy, Deputy Director of the Foreign Investment Department (Ministry of Finance), in the process of institutionalizing Resolution 10-NQ/TW, the Prime Minister directed the Ministry of Finance to play a coordinating role at the national level. Accordingly, core areas will prioritize attracting projects with high technology, innovation, and high added value. Projects with lower technological content will be directed to suitable areas, including suburban areas and regions with significant development potential.
 "This approach aims to allocate FDI flows more rationally, create development momentum for many localities, and increase the spillover effect of the FDI sector. At the same time, this idea has also been institutionalized in the amended Investment Law," Ms. Thuy said.
 Currently, according to Ms. Thuy, Vietnam is negotiating with a large-scale foreign investor and including specific conditions in the incentive package. Accordingly, this investor will benefit from tax and electricity cost support policies, but must also fulfill commitments regarding technology transfer and human resource training. Specifically, this investor is required to transfer approximately 20 technologies in fields where Vietnamese businesses are capable of adopting them, and to participate in training human resources for Vietnam.
 Ms. Thuy emphasized that this approach will be implemented through specific negotiation packages, in which each incentive package will come with corresponding conditions and commitments from the investor. The general principle is that incentives will be granted only to the extent that commitments are fulfilled. This approach aims to ensure that investment incentive policies truly create value for the economy, rather than being based solely on the size of registered capital.

articles.title: Once shunned, Myanmar's military-backed leader gets red carpet welcome in Malaysia - Awani International
articles.summary: Once shunned, Myanmar's military-backed leader gets red carpet welcome in Malaysia  Awani International
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Myanmar's junta chief-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing arrived in Malaysia on Wednesday for talks with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, as the military-backed leader once shunned by regional nations seeks international legitimacy.
The two-day visit comes as Malaysia pushes ahead with a controversial move to repatriate thousands of Myanmar nationals, despite warnings from the United Nations and rights groups that returnees could face serious danger amid a raging civil war.
"The visit provides the prime minister with an opportunity to sustain his direct engagement with Myanmar," the Malaysian government said in a statement on Tuesday.
Key issues include the "voluntary, dignified and safe repatriation of Myanmar nationals of all ethnic groups who have been in Malaysia illegally," it added.
Myanmar has been in turmoil since Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup in 2021, triggering a nationwide civil war that has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million.
The military engineered a widely criticised election that allowed Min Aung Hlaing, who is subject to a raft of Western sanctions, to take up a civilian role — a transition that has sparked some moves towards re-engagement with Myanmar.
Although Min Aung Hlaing and other senior Myanmar officials have been excluded from summits of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) since 2021 over their failure to implement an ASEAN-brokered peace roadmap, individual countries in the region have moved to rebuild ties with Naypyitaw.
Since formally becoming president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has visited ASEAN members Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam, and also made trips to China, India, Russia and Belarus.
Min Aung Hlaing was accorded a guard of honour upon his arrival on Wednesday afternoon at Kuala Lumpur International Airport, where he was greeted by Malaysia's trade minister Johari Abdul Ghani, state news agency Bernama reported.
On Thursday, he is expected to receive a formal welcoming ceremony at Anwar's office complex, before attending a bilateral meeting and an official luncheon with the prime minister, Bernama said.
DOMESTIC PRESSURE
Muslim-majority Malaysia had been one of the biggest critics of a brutal 2017 military crackdown in Myanmar's Rakhine state that saw thousands of ethnic Rohingya Muslims flee across the border to seek refuge in neighbouring Bangladesh.
Public sentiment in Malaysia however began turning against Rohingya refugees during the COVID-19 pandemic, when they were accused of spreading the virus and taking away jobs from locals.
A fresh wave of online hate speech and misinformation targeting the Rohingya earlier this year has renewed scrutiny and pressure on refugees and other undocumented migrants in Malaysia, which is not a signatory to the UN refugee convention.
Last month, Anwar said in a podcast that he would invite Min Aung Hlaing for an official visit if Myanmar accepted the return of thousands of Rohingya refugees.
"Under pressure to send refugees back, Anwar needs Naypyitaw's cooperation, and a visit is the price," said Richard Horsey, senior Asia adviser at the International Crisis Group.
"He says this is not recognition, but Min Aung Hlaing will present it as exactly that."
Malaysia has deported around 10,000 Myanmar nationals since January, according to Anwar, who said Myanmar authorities had given assurances those returning would not be harmed.
Although Malaysia has said the repatriations are strictly voluntary, the UN has raised concerns about the move, warning that people sent back to Myanmar may face serious risks.
Rights groups have also urged Malaysia to halt the returns, citing the ongoing violence and risk of forced conscription.
There are about 193,000 registered refugees and asylum seekers from Myanmar in Malaysia, according to UN data.
DEADLY AIRSTRIKES CONTINUE
Despite repeated calls for an end to the violence, including from the 11-member ASEAN grouping, the civil war in Myanmar continues unabated.
The Myanmar military has carried out several airstrikes within the last fortnight in Rakhine state, where it is battling a rebel group, killing at least 58 people and injuring dozens of others, including at a busy market.
The attack was the deadliest since a December hospital bombing and drew condemnation from UN Secretary-General António Guterres.
In a statement to Reuters, ASEAN's current chair, the Philippines, also expressed concern over the airstrike.
"Nothing in the region's response gives Naypyitaw any reason to think they will come at a diplomatic cost, including Min Aung Hlaing's red carpet in Kuala Lumpur," said Crisis Group's Horsey.

articles.title: Welcoming FDI Inflows - Final Part: Connecting to Create New Value - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Welcoming FDI Inflows - Final Part: Connecting to Create New Value  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
To attract FDI, industrial parks need to integrate production facilities with suitable transportation, housing, and services. These factors will determine whether an investment location can meet the long-term needs of businesses and workers.
Beyond supply chains, operational capabilities, and industrial symbiosis, the next question facing industrial parks is how to connect with what lies outside the factory fence. Many argue that Vietnam is shifting from a low-cost manufacturing destination to a strategic regional manufacturing hub, where demand is no longer limited to traditional industrial land but has expanded to integrated development models.
To clarify these changes, a reporter from the News and Nation newspaper interviewed Ms. Trang Le, General Director and Senior Director of Research and Consulting at JLL Vietnam.
Madam, what new opportunities are emerging for Vietnam's industrial real estate sector due to the influx of investment capital?
Vietnam continues to have a favorable foundation for attracting investment. In the first two quarters of 2026, total registered foreign investment reached approximately US$34.7 billion, a 61% increase compared to the same period last year; implemented capital reached approximately US$13 billion, an 11% increase. During the same period, GDP increased by approximately 8.2%, and export turnover increased by 21%. These indicators show that investment, production, and trade continue to support the market.
Opportunities also arise from shifts in industries. Beyond traditional manufacturing, demand is expanding into high technology, pharmaceuticals, research and development, and data centers. These activities require investment locations that align with the company's long-term strategy.
Vietnam has advantages in terms of geographical location, a network of free trade agreements, and a domestic market. Coupled with infrastructure upgrades, these factors help businesses integrate their operations into regional production networks. Therefore, developers need to view opportunities by identifying which industry sectors and functions their location best suits.
Investors now have more location options, but why do industrial land rental prices still vary so significantly between regions, Madam?
The differentiation is linked to the conditions of each location, especially connectivity. Within the key markets surveyed by JLL, the North has approximately 13,000 hectares of operational industrial land in 75 industrial parks, with an occupancy rate of 82.4%. The South has approximately 28,100 hectares in 141 industrial parks, with an occupancy rate of 84.1%. These figures are for the surveyed markets, not for all industrial parks nationwide.
Industrial land lease prices in the North range from approximately 120-180 USD/m², while in the South they range from 100-320 USD/m², calculated for the entire lease term. Areas near international seaports, airports, or major transportation routes still command higher prices than the average.
Such a price range indicates that businesses have multiple options, but each option comes with different conditions. Therefore, the price needs to be considered in relation to location and accessibility to transportation networks and markets. For investors, the advantages of the location must be demonstrated by the actual connections that the business can utilize.
With expanding transportation infrastructure creating opportunities for production, what should these new locations do to become long-term choices for FDI investors?
First, it is necessary to determine the role of the location within the overall development network. With the addition of expressways, ring roads, or transportation hubs, businesses may consider areas outside of traditional industrial centers. However, the prospects of a location must be viewed in conjunction with existing conditions and long-term development directions.
You may also like
By 2030, JLL forecasts that surveyed markets in the North could add approximately 5,000 hectares of industrial land, while the South could add over 6,000 hectares. In the North, Hai Phong leads in future supply, with four industrial parks already under construction in May 2026 alone. Hanoi also commenced construction on two new industrial parks, adding to the development space.
In the South, Long Thanh International Airport, Ho Chi Minh City's Ring Road 3, the Ben Luc - Long Thanh expressway, and logistics hubs are expected to expand regional connectivity. These changes create more options while also requiring industrial parks to be viewed within a broader economic context.
New land plots need to be connected to transportation networks and have conditions that support long-term operations. The attractiveness of a location comes from these factors, not just from the added land area.
Many projects combine industrial, residential, and commercial elements. Why, despite having all these components, has a complete ecosystem not yet been created, Madam?
The issue lies in whether the components truly fit together. Bringing industry, housing, and commerce into a single project creates spatial cohesion. To become an ecosystem, these components must meet the needs of the relevant user groups.
Developers need to understand the income, housing needs, and affordability of workers in industrial zones. In reality, there is still a gap between factory workers and the target customer group for residential and commercial properties.
If the residential area is developed for a different customer group, workers may still not find suitable housing, even if the housing is right near their workplace. In that case, the buildings stand next to each other but do not truly complement each other.
This is one of the reasons why some integrated models have not been as effective as expected. Whether a project is complete or not should be judged by its ability to meet real needs, not just by its list of works.
According to her, what should developers consider to ensure that housing and services are truly suitable for people working in industrial zones?
In my opinion, the first step is to identify who the product is for. Workers, skilled laborers, and professionals have different living needs. Analyzing the characteristics of the workforce, income, and ability to pay will help investors choose the right product.
Housing near the workplace may not necessarily solve the needs if workers lack access to it. The same applies to commercial amenities; they may be available but not meet their needs. Therefore, the development of these components must be linked to the very people who will work and live in the area.
You may also like
Workers' housing, expert apartments, and community amenities are part of the "soft infrastructure" that helps attract and retain workers, especially those from other localities and foreign experts.
Understanding the users correctly is essential for investors to arrange the components appropriately. Only when the workplace and living conditions are integrated can the integrated model effectively meet long-term needs.
Furthermore, developers need to consider the existing infrastructure, amenities, and services in the surrounding area to connect with and support the project. Some areas already partially meet the living needs of workers. Recognizing this helps investors understand what is lacking in the area before deciding to invest further.
If each industrial park builds its own self-contained system without integration with the broader economic space, investment efficiency and synergy will be limited. Placing the project within the context of the entire area will help to better define the role of each component.
For new industrial zones, attractiveness needs to be built on the connection between production facilities, transportation networks, and suitable living conditions. When these components serve the right needs and support each other, the new investment location has a foundation for long-term business and worker development.

articles.title: Malaysia's RM510bil 2027 Budget to draw quality investments: Banking executives - NST Online
articles.summary: Malaysia's RM510bil 2027 Budget to draw quality investments: Banking executives  NST Online
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's RM510 billion 2027 Budget is expected to attract high-value investments, support business growth and boost household incomes, banking executives said.
CIMB Group chief executive officer Novan Amirudin said the country's economic reform agenda sought to strengthen competitiveness, attract quality investments and foster innovation while ensuring growth translated into better opportunities and living standards.
He said fiscal responsibility and common prosperity must go hand in hand, with reforms focusing on industrial upgrading, infrastructure, energy transition, skills development and financial inclusion.
For the banking sector, these measures would create opportunities to mobilise capital towards priority sectors while supporting businesses and households.
"Banks become not only beneficiaries of reform, but active partners in advancing sustainable growth, economic resilience and common prosperity," he said.
HIGH-VALUE INDUSTRIES TO DRIVE GROWTH
OCBC Bank (Malaysia) Bhd chief executive officer Tan Chor Sen said the budget's emphasis on higher-value industries would strengthen Malaysia's economic position.
Developments in Penang and Kulim's semiconductor and advanced manufacturing ecosystems, alongside Tanjung Malim's emergence as a regional automotive hub, could help local companies integrate into sophisticated supply chains and move up the value chain.
The RM25 billion in domestic investments mobilised by government-linked investment companies under the GEAR-uP initiative would further support this direction.
Tan also welcomed enhancements to the Global Services Hub incentive, saying Malaysia was well positioned to attract more foreign direct investment amid disruptions to global supply chains.
Measures to improve small and medium enterprises' competitiveness, including tax incentives, technology and productivity investments, and expanded financing, would help businesses scale up and explore overseas markets.
The RM60 million allocation to the Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation and RM1 billion in financing from Bank Pembangunan Malaysia Bhd for export-oriented SMEs will support companies seeking opportunities abroad.
SKILLS & FISCAL DISCIPLINE REMAIN KEY
Mushahid Syed, interim chief executive officer, head of coverage and chief financial officer of Standard Chartered Malaysia, said the budget's focus on investment, skills development and higher-value industries would reinforce Malaysia's position as a regional trade hub.
He said the commitment to narrow the fiscal deficit to 3.3 per cent of gross domestic product in 2027, alongside federal revenue projected at RM380.8 billion, sent a positive signal to investors and financial markets.
"The continued thrust on NIMP 2030, National Energy Transition Roadmap, National Semiconductor Strategy, digital and AI, and supply chain diversification gives businesses confidence," he said.
Mushahid said the RM8 billion allocation for technical and vocational education and training, three million training opportunities through HRD Corp and 30,000 targeted employment opportunities under Bakat Madani will help develop the workforce needed to sustain economic transformation.
He added that stronger workforce capabilities would be essential for Malaysia to attract quality investments and move up global value chains.
SMEs & GREEN INVESTMENT
Mushahid said SME support was important as businesses navigated geopolitical uncertainty and changing market conditions.

articles.title: Critical considerations for economic growth - Vietnam Economic Times
articles.summary: Critical considerations for economic growth  Vietnam Economic Times
articles.full_text:
The Vietnamese Government remains committed to high growth while maintaining macro-economic stability. First-half 2026 GDP growth of 8.18 per cent was the highest in the first-half period in any year since 1998. Reaching the government’s 10 per cent annual target will therefore require year-on-year growth of 11.59 per cent in the second half. Developments in the first eight months, however, point to several challenges that require closer attention and appropriate policy responses.
Inflation came in at 4.45 per cent in the first eight months, leaving little room to stay within the official 4.5 per cent target. With prices typically rising faster toward year-end, inflation could exceed 5 per cent, surpassing the target approved by the 15th National Assembly (NA) at its tenth session on November 13, 2025.
Limits of investment
Investment, particularly public investment, is expected to play an important role in driving growth. Total social investment during 2026-2030 is estimated at around VND38,500 trillion ($1.5 trillion), or 2.21-times the level in the previous five-year period. The investment-to-GDP ratio will need to increase to around 40 per cent, equivalent to approximately $280 billion annually, which is a substantial requirement.
But the issue is not simply how much capital can be mobilized. It is also about the maturity, cost, and allocation of that capital, and whether projects can generate sufficient economic returns and useful output while maintaining an appropriate balance of inputs.
Beyond increasing investment, Vietnam needs to raise productivity and the amount of growth generated by each unit of capital. This means reducing the Incremental Capital-Output Ratio (ICOR) from its current level of around 6 to approximately 4. That will be challenging as localities compete to develop airports, seaports, industrial parks, and major urban areas.
The investment race is also playing out across ministries and sectors, raising concerns about excess capacity and low utilization. Some projects involve enormous capital outlays but are used only for a handful of events each year, such as stadiums and theaters, while existing facilities remain underutilized. Public investment is concentrated largely in transport infrastructure, while private capital continues to flow mainly into real estate and urban development. Direct investment in core technologies such as AI, semiconductors, robotics, and R&D remains limited.
Even privately-funded projects warrant scrutiny. Land is a finite resource, while private projects typically combine equity, accounting for around 20-30 per cent of capital, with funds raised from the public. Their efficiency therefore, needs to be assessed not only from the investor’s perspective but also in terms of their broader economic impact.
Railway development illustrates the importance of project and infrastructure planning. Current debates include whether Hanoi should build a new central station in Ngoc Hoi or retain the existing Hanoi Station in the city center.
Another often-overlooked issue is the need for long-term capital. Large infrastructure projects cannot generate revenue to service debt during construction, while projects such as expressways can have a payback period of 15-20 years. Yet they often rely on commercial bank loans for 70-80 per cent of their funding, with banks using predominantly short-term deposits to finance long-term lending.
Vietnam’s capital market is not yet capable of meeting this demand, leaving commercial banks to bear much of the burden of long-term financing. Medium and long-term funds account for only around 20 per cent of total deposits, while the banking system’s overall capital adequacy ratio (CAR) is around 12 per cent.
Unless the bond and equity markets are developed further to mobilize more long-term capital, the maturity mismatch between funding and lending that has accumulated over the years could increase systemic risks in the banking sector and add to inflationary pressure.
Credit under pressure
To support growth while maintaining macro-economic stability, the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) has set a system-wide credit growth target of around 15 per cent for 2026. As of August 28, outstanding credit stood at approximately VND20,500 trillion ($788.5 billion), up 10.24 per cent from the end of 2025. The 15 per cent target may therefore require technical measures to exclude certain credit exposures.
The SBV has also repeatedly relaxed credit limits. Circular No. 08/2026/TT-NHNN, issued on May 15, 2026, changed the loan-to-deposit ratio (LDR) calculation by allowing 20 per cent of State Treasury term deposits to be included in the funding base. The ratio increased to 50 per cent from August 1, applicable through July 31, 2028, affecting both monetary and fiscal policy.
As of end-March 2026, State Treasury deposits at banks totaled VND626.7 trillion ($24.1 billion), with more than 99 per cent held at four State-owned commercial banks (SOCBs). While this does not change the amount of money in the economy, it eases liquidity pressure and increases the lending capacity of these banks. It may also widen deposit rate differentials between State-owned and private banks, complicating monetary policy management and raising questions about whether different funding conditions warrant different regulatory treatment.
On May 30, the SBV permitted 25 banks to exclude additional lending for social housing, industrial parks, and export processing zones from their 2026 real estate credit growth limits, though such loans remain subject to overall credit limits.
Circular No. 25/2026/TT-NHNN, issued on June 22, raised the share of short-term funds that can be used for medium and long-term lending from 30 per cent to 40 per cent for LDR calculations. While this provides banks with additional funding capacity, it also increases maturity mismatch risks. In the first half of 2026, the system-wide LDR was already around 115 per cent; well above the SBV’s 85 per cent regulatory threshold under Circular No. 22/2019/TT-NHNN.
The SBV’s Official Letter No. 5386/NHNN-TD, also issued on June 22, further attracted attention by excluding loans to 18 projects of three major private economic groups from credit growth limits. The SBV described them as “key national projects with broad regional spillover effects and an impact on the economy.”
Supporters argue that the measure enables large domestic companies to participate in strategic infrastructure projects, strengthen domestic corporate capacity, and reduce reliance on FDI, following a path previously taken by Japan and South Korea. However, eight of the 18 projects are real estate developments, including the Bai Dat Do mixed-use urban area, the Nui Ong Quan mixed-use ecotourism urban area, and the Rach Chiec National Sports Complex. None are energy or technology projects covered by priority policies.
Transparent criteria for selecting eligible projects are therefore important. Concentrating credit on key projects without clear selection criteria could undermine efforts to build a healthy business environment and weaken credit discipline.
The SBV is also seeking comments on a draft circular implementing Resolution No. 258/2025/QH15 on special mechanisms for major projects in the capital. The draft would raise lending limits to a single borrower and to a borrower and its related parties to 38 per cent and 52 per cent of a bank’s equity capital, respectively, or nearly 2.92 and 2.48-times the current limits.
Under the Law on Credit Institutions, the limits until January 1, 2027 are 13 per cent for a single borrower and 21 per cent for a borrower and related parties. Though the NA’s resolution permits certain projects to apply special mechanisms through a prescribed approval process, a circular alone cannot authorize lending beyond statutory limits.
The proposed relaxation also raises systemic risk concerns. Excessive exposure to a single project or borrower could threaten individual banks and, if confidence deteriorates, potentially trigger broader deposit withdrawals. Greater transparency over bank lending above statutory limits, the projects involved, and the extent of any excess would therefore be important.
Interest rate and exchange rate challenge
The government’s call for genuine lending rate reductions based on lower funding costs is justified, as businesses cannot generate sufficient profits to service excessively high borrowing costs of more than 10 per cent per annum. However, interest rate reductions have yet to prove sustainable in practice because monetary policy has focused primarily on treating the symptoms rather than addressing the root causes. Strong demand for investment capital, combined with slow growth in deposits - and even a decline in corporate deposits - is putting upward pressure on interest rates.
To secure funding for public investment projects as well as public-private partnership (PPP) projects, the government has had to increase bond issuance, pushing up government bond yields. The yield on ten-year government bonds currently ranges from 4.3-4.5 per cent per year, up 0.5-0.9 percentage points from the same period of 2025, contributing to higher interest rates across the economy.
As with public investment capital, the root structural issue is the maturity mismatch in credit funding, and regulations have recently been loosened further. Medium and long-term funds account for only 20 per cent of total deposits, yet banks are now allowed to use as much as 40 per cent of short-term funds to provide medium and long-term loans. The more unstable economic policies become in ways that disadvantage production and business activity, the more difficult it will be to mobilize long-term capital for development and the harder it will be to bring lending rates down.
