articles.title: A measure of the global competitiveness of Vietnamese businesses. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: A measure of the global competitiveness of Vietnamese businesses.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
(Dan Tri Newspaper) - Deputy Minister of Home Affairs Nguyen Thi Ha commented that the "Go Global Bac Ninh 2026" forum suggests a broader approach: the journey to the world can entirely begin with a factory in Bac Ninh.
On the morning of October 10th, Dan Tri newspaper, in collaboration with the Department of Industry and Trade of Bac Ninh City and the Bac Ninh City Industrial Production Association, organized the "Go Global Bac Ninh 2026" forum with the theme "Enhancing Capacity - Connecting Supply Chains - Developing Markets". Deputy Minister of Home Affairs Nguyen Thi Ha attended and spoke at the forum.
Also attending were Standing Vice Chairwoman of the Bac Ninh City People's Council Tran Thi Hang, Vice Chairman of the Bac Ninh City People's Committee Pham Van Thinh, Deputy Director of the Import-Export Department, Ministry of Industry and Trade Trinh Thi Thu Hien, along with representatives from the leadership of various departments, agencies, commune and ward People's Committees, and leaders of business associations and federations in Bac Ninh City.
Global competitiveness of Vietnamese businesses
In her opening remarks, Deputy Minister Nguyen Thi Ha stated that the forum was being held at a very significant time. Vietnam is becoming a destination for many international corporations in the fields of electronics, semiconductors, and high technology. Along with the influx of investment capital and the expansion of production by FDI enterprises, a huge market is emerging domestically: the demand for Vietnamese suppliers capable of participating in global production chains.
For Bac Ninh, this opportunity is even more significant as the city has been and continues to be one of the major centers for electronics, high technology, and industrial production.
In that context, Deputy Minister Nguyen Thi Ha stated: "The important question now is not only how many large corporations we attract to invest, but also how many Vietnamese businesses have the capacity to enter the supply chains of those corporations? Furthermore, where do Vietnamese businesses stand and what is their position in the global value chain? That is also a pressing issue that Go Global Bac Ninh 2026 addresses."
You may also like
Deputy Minister Nguyen Thi Ha reiterated that at the 2025 ESG Forum, many experts and leaders of corporations and groups suggested expanding the forum to local areas. And this year, that has become a reality with the event taking place in Bac Ninh city.
Go Global has long been understood as bringing Vietnamese goods abroad. But today's program suggests a broader and more practical approach: the journey to the world can entirely begin from a factory in Bac Ninh.
When a Vietnamese business becomes a supplier to a global corporation manufacturing in Vietnam, that business has essentially entered the global value chain. This is the path of "on-site globalization." The second path is "cross-border globalization"—bringing Vietnamese products, services, and brands directly to international markets and consumers. These two paths are different, but they share one common point: to enter the global market, a business must first possess global competitiveness.
To advance further on that path, according to the Deputy Minister of Home Affairs, businesses must simultaneously meet many factors such as: quality, technology, productivity, delivery schedule, management, human resources, R&D, data, and increasingly high international standards.
Human resources are a crucial factor.
Throughout this journey, Deputy Minister Nguyen Thi Ha also paid special attention to the human factor. Machinery and technology can be imported and transferred. However, a team of skilled engineers, workers, and managers capable of working to international standards and a professional management culture must be built through a process. Therefore, human resource development must precede or at least accompany the process of upgrading technology and participating in the global value chain.
The Deputy Minister highly appreciated that the workshop went beyond mere presentations and discussions. Based on expert opinions, business feedback, and survey results, the Deputy Minister of the Ministry of Interior learned that the Organizing Committee plans to compile these into a "Go Global Bac Ninh 2027 Action Program." This is very significant.
You may also like
Because the ultimate value of a forum lies not only in what we say to each other. According to the Deputy Minister, value must be measured by what happens after the conference. That is, how many businesses are connected? How many businesses raise their standards? How many new Vietnamese suppliers are selected? How many Vietnamese products find new markets? A Vietnamese business's global journey can begin today, right from its factory in Bac Ninh.
This program is part of the ESG Vietnam Forum 2026 series of activities themed "Seizing Opportunities - Leading Growth".
The event brought together representatives from the government, semiconductor experts, global technology corporations, Vietnamese businesses in the supply chain, Amazon Global Selling, banks, and the Private Economic Development Research Board... Each speaker offered a different perspective on the "Go Global" journey of businesses in Bac Ninh.
This event aims for a broader approach to "Go Global". For Vietnamese businesses, the path to the world doesn't just start with exports, but can begin right from their domestic factories, by becoming suppliers to FDI corporations and international supply chains operating in Vietnam.

Thailand began hosting the 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group in Bangkok on October 12, bringing together around 17,000 participants from 191 countries for discussions on the global economy, finance and development.
The meetings, running through October 18 at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center, bring together finance ministers, central bank governors, government and business executives, civil society organisations, academics, journalists and other international figures.
Discussions during the week will cover major global challenges including poverty, inequality, climate change, public debt, financial technology, digital assets and cyber risks to the financial system.
The gathering is intended to provide a platform for countries and international institutions to exchange views on policies aimed at strengthening economic stability and supporting sustainable development.
Thailand is hosting the Annual Meetings for the second time, 35 years after it first hosted the gathering in 1991.
The host-country theme is “Thailand’s New Horizons: Empowering People, Building Resilience”, reflecting Thailand’s focus on people-centred development and strengthening resilience to economic and financial risks.
The government is also using the meetings to showcase Thailand’s economic potential, attract foreign investment and hold bilateral discussions aimed at expanding international cooperation.
Hosting the event is expected to generate an estimated THB1.05-2.25 billion in domestic economic activity, based on more than 15,000 participants staying for an average of seven to 10 days and spending about THB10,000-15,000 per person per day.
Spending is expected to benefit tourism, hotels, restaurants, services and local products.
Leading international figures scheduled to participate during the week include IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva and World Bank Group President Ajay Banga.
Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam and President of the Swiss Confederation Guy Parmelin are also among the senior international figures attending events in Bangkok.
Other participants include US Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh, European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development Secretary-General Mathias Cormann, World Trade Organization Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala and European Commissioner for Economy and Productivity Valdis Dombrovskis.
Senior business executives include DBS Group CEO Tan Su Shan, Grab Group CEO and co-founder Anthony Tan, and Trip.com Group CEO Jane Sun.
Thai speakers and participants include Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas and Bank of Thailand Governor Vitai Ratanakorn.
Also taking part are Veerathai Santiprabhob, chairman of the Thailand Development Research Institute; Narongchai Akrasanee, chairman of the Institute for Strategic Policy Foundation; and Suthiphand Chirathivat of Chulalongkorn University.
Other Thai participants include Vice Minister for Finance Santitarn Sathirathai, Vice Minister for Commerce Kirida Bhaopichitr, Revenue Department official Saowakon Meesang and KASIKORNBANK CEO Kattiya Indaravijaya.

Speakers include Banga, Georgieva, Tharman and Ekniti, alongside government officials, technology experts and innovators.
Another opening-day highlight is the launch of the Thailand Pavilion from 4.30pm to 5.30pm.
Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul is due to join Ekniti, Vitai, Banga and Georgieva at the opening.

articles.title: The metro station is just the starting point; what determines TOD's success? - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The metro station is just the starting point; what determines TOD's success?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City are accelerating urban development based on the TOD (Transit-Oriented Development) model. Along with this process, the real estate market is also undergoing significant shifts to adapt to this development model that prioritizes public transportation.
 However, according to Cushman & Wakefield, an area with a metro station and surrounding real estate projects is not enough to form a true TOD (Transit-Oriented Development). This model is only truly effective when public transportation is integrated with land-use planning, living spaces, jobs, services, and economic activities.
 TOD needs more than just apartments; it requires a multi-functional ecosystem.
 According to Cushman & Wakefield, the first condition for TOD (Transit-Oriented Development) to be effective is that land use planning must be sufficiently diversified. A TOD area that focuses solely on apartment development will struggle to create jobs and sustainable economic activities. Instead, there needs to be a balanced combination of housing, offices, retail, hotels, healthcare, education , public services, green spaces, and community amenities.
 The diversity of functions allows the area to generate a flow of people and economic activity across various time frames, rather than being crowded only at certain times of the day.
 "Close to the metro" isn't enough; it has to be conveniently accessible on foot.
 Walkability is another crucial factor for TOD. According to Cushman & Wakefield, TOD is not simply about developing real estate "near the metro." Residents must be able to walk safely, conveniently, and comfortably from the station to their homes, workplaces, shops, schools, and public spaces.
 If passengers disembark from the metro but still have to rely on motorbikes or cars for the final leg of their journey, the effectiveness of the model will be significantly limited. Therefore, the connection between the station and surrounding destinations needs to be viewed as part of the TOD (Transit-Oriented Development) system, rather than just seeing the station as a factor that increases the value of nearby real estate.
 High population density must go hand in hand with urban quality.
 A TOD (Transit-Oriented Development) area also needs a sufficiently high development density to generate user traffic, service demand, and commercial efficiency. However, this density must be controlled and accompanied by commensurate infrastructure capacity. According to Cushman & Wakefield, technical infrastructure, social infrastructure, public spaces, and operational management capacity must all be considered in a coordinated manner.
 If TOD (Transit-Oriented Development) only increases land use efficiency without improving urban quality, it can put more pressure on infrastructure and people's lives instead of addressing existing problems.
 Transparency in land development and redevelopment mechanisms.
 Another crucial factor is the need for clear and transparent land development and redevelopment mechanisms. TOD (Transit-Oriented Development) areas often involve multiple owners, complex demographics, and urban spatial restructuring needs. Without clear mechanisms for compensation, public-private partnerships, and value-sharing from land, investors will find it difficult to make long-term commitments. Furthermore, each TOD area needs to be positioned according to a specific economic function that aligns with its unique advantages.
 Businesses don't choose a location solely because it has a metro. Access to labor and customers, operating costs, infrastructure quality, service ecosystem, and commercial image can all influence the decision to locate a business. Depending on the advantages of each area, TODs (Transit-Oriented Development Centers) can be oriented towards becoming centers for finance, technology, education, healthcare , retail, urban logistics, or tourism.
 When these conditions are met simultaneously, TOD can move beyond simply increasing land prices to become a driver of attracting businesses, creating jobs, and boosting local economic growth.
 Population density and new jobs are important indicators.
 According to Cushman & Wakefield, approximately 10 years is a sufficient timeframe to assess the success of a TOD (Transit-Oriented Development) model. Population density and employment are key indicators of effectiveness. Compared to real estate prices, these indicators more accurately reflect the actual operational capacity of an area. Land prices may increase due to expectations, speculation, or supply scarcity, but price increases do not necessarily mean a TOD has been successful.
 When people genuinely choose to live there, businesses proactively establish offices, shops, or service facilities, and workers regularly commute to the area using public transport, that's when it becomes a true economic hub. At that point, the area not only has higher property values but also generates a sustainable flow of people, jobs, capital, and service demand.
 In other words, the ultimate goal of TOD is not to increase land prices, but to improve accessibility, land use efficiency, and urban productivity.
 TOD does not mean real estate near a train station.
 According to Cushman & Wakefield, some misunderstandings about TOD (Transit-Oriented Development) still exist in Vietnam. The most common misconception is that TOD is synonymous with real estate development near metro stations. In reality, "near the metro" is only a prerequisite. True TOD is an integrated urban development model based on public transportation, where the station becomes the central hub for organizing living, working, commercial, service, and community spaces.
 A project located near a train station but lacking pedestrian access, transit facilities, mixed-use functions, public amenities, and appropriate density cannot be considered a TOD (Transit-Oriented Development) project. If the project focuses solely on building and selling real estate, it is primarily development benefiting from transportation infrastructure, rather than a complete TOD model.
 TOD can create new growth centers.
 If implemented correctly, TOD (Transit-Oriented Development) can help form new growth centers, reduce pressure on existing central areas, improve access to housing, and enhance urban competitiveness. Conversely, if planning is inconsistent, TOD risks creating only a surge in land prices around train stations without delivering commensurate improvements in quality of life and economic value for the locality.
 Therefore, the value of TOD (Transit-Oriented Development) lies not in the distance from a real estate project to a metro station, but in its ability to connect public transportation with living spaces, jobs, services, and economic activities. When these elements work together, the station truly becomes the nucleus of a new urban center.

articles.title: The capital market a wealthier Vietnam needs - Theinvestor
articles.summary: The capital market a wealthier Vietnam needs  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Following its upgrade, Vietnam's stock market has an opportunity to attract greater international capital flows. Alongside the country's ambition for double-digit economic growth, another need is emerging at home: Vietnamese people are increasingly able to save and want their wealth to grow with the economy, without turning investing into a second job.
Vietnam's market status upgrade on September 21, 2026 raises a question that goes beyond foreign investment, stock valuations or capital flows from international funds: Can the capital market serve both businesses seeking the resources to expand and households gaining the means to accumulate wealth?
The 14th National Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam set a target of average annual GDP growth of at least 10% during 2026-2030, with GDP per capita reaching approximately $8,500 by the end of the decade. The Politburo's Resolution 68-NQ/TW affirmed the private sector's role as a driving force of the economy, while Resolution 57-NQ/TW seeks to advance science, technology and innovation.
Achieving these ambitions will require a financing structure capable of supporting long-term development. High-tech factories and data infrastructure need patient capital. For growth to be sustainable, the economy cannot rely solely on bank lending. It also needs equity capital and financial institutions capable of supporting businesses through successive economic cycles.
On the other side are the savings households set aside from each paycheck. For a family, this is far from an abstract pool of capital. It represents a child's education, financial provisions for ageing parents, a home or the years when employment income is no longer available. The capital market can fulfil its role only when it connects these two needs.
The upgrade opens the door, but market depth remains the test
On September 18, the Ministry of Finance and the State Securities Commission of Vietnam (SSC), in cooperation with FTSE Russell, held a conference in Hanoi to celebrate Vietnam's entry into the FTSE Russell Global Equity Index Series (FTSE GEIS). From September 21, Vietnam officially became a Secondary Emerging Market under FTSE Russell's classification, ending eight years on its upgrade watchlist.
FTSE Russell is incorporating Vietnamese equities into its indices in four phases, with the process scheduled for completion by September 2027. Approximately $20 trillion in assets worldwide use FTSE Russell indices as benchmarks. That figure, however, does not represent capital committed to Vietnam. Actual inflows will depend on the country's index weightings, the accessibility of its equities, and individual fund managers' investment decisions.
At the conference, Minister of Finance Ngo Van Tuan outlined three priorities for reform: improving corporate governance and market discipline, enhancing investor access, and establishing the legal foundations for new investment models and products. FTSE Russell CEO Fiona Bassett emphasized that a market's development is reflected not only in its index classification, but also in the scale, depth and resilience of its financial system.
An upgrade creates opportunities; it does not guarantee a sustained rise in share prices. To retain long-term capital, Vietnam will also need transparent companies, quality listed securities and trustworthy asset management institutions.
Reforms have not stopped with the upgrade. At a Ministry of Finance press briefing on October 6, SSC Vice Chairman Hoang Van Thu said regulators were studying proposals to divide stocks into separate market segments based on quality, foreign investor accessibility and free-float ratios.
They were also considering trading through the lunch break, adjustments to daily price fluctuation limits and changes to order-matching mechanisms. Deputy Minister of Finance Nguyen Duc Chi stressed the importance of safeguarding systemic stability before introducing any changes.
At the Vietnam Fund Awards 2026, SSC Chairwoman Vu Thi Chan Phuong also emphasized the development of investment products aligned with people's long-term savings needs and a greater role for professional investment institutions. Over the past decade, assets under management at Vietnamese fund management companies have grown by more than 20% annually on average.
A wealthier society needs new ways to invest
As incomes improve, Vietnamese people's investment needs are also changing. UOB's ASEAN Consumer Sentiment Study 2026 found that 89% of Vietnamese respondents save more than 10% of their monthly income, the highest proportion among five ASEAN markets surveyed. Meanwhile, 63% allocate more than 10% of their annual income to investments. Behind these figures is a desire not merely to preserve savings, but to see them grow over time.
As wealth increases, financial needs become more diverse. Young people may be saving for their first home; families may be preparing to pay for their children's education; and middle-aged workers may be thinking about the years after retirement. They may believe in the prospects of Vietnamese businesses, but that does not necessarily mean they have time to research individual stocks, monitor market screens or adjust their portfolios.
The market already offers a range of investment options. Buying individual stocks provides direct ownership and control over investment decisions. Open-ended funds allow investors to entrust portfolio management to professionals, while exchange-traded funds (ETFs) provide exposure to baskets of stocks tracking an index. As more people gain the means to build wealth, the range of available products must also become more diverse, particularly for those who want direct ownership without having to shoulder every aspect of portfolio management themselves.
This is where Direct Indexing can offer an additional option. Under this approach, investors directly own the individual stocks in a portfolio constructed around an index or an index-based strategy. Technology and investment professionals support portfolio allocation, monitoring and rebalancing according to predetermined rules. Ownership remains with the client, while portfolio management follows a consistent methodology.
In the United States, Direct Indexing is gaining traction in the wealth management industry. A survey of 400 financial advisors published by FTSE Russell in September 2026 found that adoption had risen from 33% to 41% over the previous year. Some 83% of respondents were either using Direct Indexing or planning to adopt it within the next 12 months. These findings indicate a growing trend in the U.S. market, not a forecast of how the model will develop in Vietnam.
Nevertheless, the model suggests a potential fit with a familiar characteristic of Vietnamese investment behavior: a preference for directly owning assets, alongside a desire to diversify risk and accumulate wealth through a disciplined approach. Direct Indexing may help reconcile these two objectives, making index-based investing possible not only through fund units, but also through portfolios of individual stocks held directly by investors.
Direct Indexing is not a replacement for ETFs, open-ended funds or individual stock investing. It can complement the existing investment ecosystem, provided that the technology, costs and quality of portfolio management meet investors' expectations. More important than the arrival of any single product is a broader shift in how the market serves the public: from creating additional trading opportunities to expanding access to long-term wealth accumulation.
A country growing wealthier needs not only more capital for its businesses, but also investment approaches that allow its people to share in the benefits of economic growth. That is when the stock market becomes genuinely relevant to everyday life: not by requiring everyone to become a professional trader, but by opening up opportunities to build wealth through the steady efforts of a lifetime of work.

Royal row tests Malaysia’s constitutional order  South China Morning PostBackdating is taboo in law — Hafiz Hassan  Malay MailMalaysia’s Royal Dispute Leaves Negeri Sembilan in Constitutional Limbo  Sri Lanka Guardian
articles.full_text:

KUALA LUMPUR - Embattled Negeri Sembilan ruler Muhriz Munawir has been invited to the Oct 13 to 15 Conference of Rulers, amid a palace feud in his state that has dragged the federal Malaysian government into a brewing constitutional crisis.
The invitation from Sultan Nazrin Azlan Shah of Perak - whose turn it is to chair the council - strengthens Muhriz’s legitimacy, which is being questioned by Negeri Sembilan’s territorial chieftains, empowered under the state’s unique constitution to elect or remove a ruler found unfit to reign.
However, Muhriz has informed Nazrin that he will attend only the pre-council meeting of Malaysia’s nine state sovereigns on Oct 13. The pre-council is not attended by Malaysia’s King, currently Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar of Johor, so as to preserve the sanctity of state-level interests before meeting federal representatives including Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.
Official sources told The Straits Times that Yang di-Pertuan Besar Muhriz is scheduled to preside over the appointment of a new chieftain, or Undang, of Jelebu on Oct 14.
“It’s a crucial event as it will give Muhriz a clear majority in Negeri Sembilan’s Dewan Keadilan dan Undang (DKU),” a source with knowledge of the crisis told ST on condition of anonymity given the sensitivity around royal affairs.
The DKU is the highest authority on the state’s Adat Perpatih, a centuries-old custom governing its feudal hierarchy. Of the four Undang, Jelebu will now be the third seen to be loyal to Muhriz. The appointment gives him more leverage against the rebellion led by his cousin, Nadzaruddin Ja’afar, who wants to replace him.
Nadzaruddin - proclaimed by three former and one current Undang as the new Yang di-Pertuan Besar, or Yamtuan - has been snubbed by Sultan Nazrin. The son of the previous Negeri Sembilan ruler has not been invited, ST has learnt, despite making repeated requests through various rulers and the state’s chief minister Ismail Lasim to secure an invitation in place of Muhriz.
Nadzaruddin has aligned himself to the rebel chieftains and UMNO - which reclaimed the state from Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan after forcing snap polls held in August. The bruising crisis has damaged the institution of the constitutional monarchy and left Negeri Sembilan without a functioning government since September.
The Undang proclaimed on April 19 that they have removed Muhriz from the throne but the constitution explicitly requires an inquiry into the Yamtuan’s alleged transgressions. This, however, was never convened. Malaysia’s Attorney General has repeatedly stated that Muhriz’s claimed dismissal was unconstitutional and he remains the sole occupant to the Negeri Sembilan throne.
Muhriz has held a public stance against corruption and abuse of power - in particular the appointment of judges - that has made him some powerful enemies amongst Malaysia’s elite. These include UMNO leaders who are spearheading the move to pardon former prime minister Najib Razak.
Muhriz has so far kept his silence despite the cloud over his legitimacy. However, that he has presided over the removal of three new Undang speaks volumes.
“He may make his feelings clear during the appointment of the Jelebu Undang on Oct 14 as it is an opportune time having been affirmed by the Conference of Rulers,” a source close to the Negeri Sembilan palace told ST.
This comes even as Negeri Sembilan UMNO chief Jalaludddin Alias has been forced to deny reports that he is planning to oust his party colleague Ismail as chief minister.
On Sept 17, Ismail claimed that his state Cabinet - formally known as executive councillors or exco - affirmed Muhriz’s removal as Yamtuan based on an April proclamation by the Undang. This is despite Ismail being sworn in as Menteri Besar before Muhriz, the day after UMNO won the Aug 1 snap polls.
But the state secretary - the top civil servant in the state bureaucracy - has cited the Attorney General’s legal opinion in refusing to gazette the Ismail administration’s decision.
On Sept 20, Muhriz sacked the exco and the bureaucracy subsequently barred them from entering the offices of the executive council.
The Menteri Besar has shifted allegiances between the two claimants to the throne, deepening the palace crisis. He filed two police reports earlier in September, seen by ST, that he was forced to sign a proclamation on Aug 3 that Muhriz was no longer Yamtuan under duress and denying that he supported the dethroning of Muhriz.
The imbroglio brings into sharp focus the increasing coupling of Malaysia’s constitutional monarchy and politics.
According to a Sept 5 statement by the chieftains - three of whom have had their positions revoked in recent months - Ismail met them on Aug 3 to gain their blessing and that of the contender to the throne, Nadzaruddin.
The chieftains said Ismail signed the proclamation removing Muhriz from the throne and paving the way for Nadzaruddin to be installed.
In a short response on Sept 6, Ismail said “the four Undang have the right to their opinion” but that he “and the state government express full loyalty to Muhriz Munawir as the Yang di-Pertuan Besar”, without confirming or denying whether he signed the proclamation.
This flies in the face of UMNO’s stance that politicians should not interfere with royal matters. It was the principle it invoked when withdrawing support for the previous chief minister Aminuddin Harun, which led to the state assembly being dissolved in June.
They had accused Aminuddin, a vice president in Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Parti Keadilan Rakyat, of interfering with Negeri Sembilan’s Adat Perpatih when he refused to sign off on the proclamation by the Undang ousting Muhriz.
The belief in UMNO is that having criticised Aminuddin for gainsaying the Undang, the public expects the party to put the matter to bed now that it has taken power in Negeri Sembilan.
Party vice-president Johari Ghani was reported as saying UMNO must clear the air on Negeri Sembilan before the campaign for the Nov 14 Melaka state polls.
“We must explain and tell the public that the parties that wants to sack Muhriz is not UMNO,” he told reporters on Oct 11.
The previous meeting of Malaysia’s nine royal houses scheduled for June was postponed by the monarchs amid uncertainty over the Negeri Sembilan throne.
Muhriz was due to chair the June conference, at a time when the issue of a renewed pardon bid by former UMNO chief Najib - currently serving a six-year term for graft involving the multi-billion dollar 1MDB saga - was a key talking point among the brother rulers, according to sources close to several royal houses.
Najib was handed a conditional house arrest in September by the Federal Territories Pardons Board chaired by Sultan Ibrahim as Agong.

articles.title: Indonesia’s strategic point is worth more than another data-centre boom - Asian Business Review
articles.summary: Indonesia’s strategic point is worth more than another data-centre boom  Asian Business Review
articles.full_text:
Indonesia’s competitive advantage will depend on whether it can turn its geography into an integrated system.
Indonesia’s next integrated digital infrastructure strategy should not begin with where to build the next data centre or how to connect more closely with Singapore. It should begin with a broader economic question: whether digitalisation will merely reinforce the geography of economic activity that already exists, or whether it can help create new centres of productivity, investment, and technological capability.
The distinction matters because Indonesia remains one of Asia’s most spatially concentrated large economies. In 2025, Indonesia’s GDP reached roughly US$1.44t ($1.8t), yet 56.93% of national output was still generated in Java, and Sulawesi contributed only 7.22%. Yet Sulawesi recorded the fastest growth amongst Indonesia’s major island groups at 6.23%, above Java’s 5.30%.
The challenge is therefore not simply to accelerate growth outside Java, but to build the infrastructure and investment density that let that growth compound.
Digital infrastructure alone will not rebalance the economy. Data centres, submarine cables, cloud platforms, and satellite gateways tend to follow existing concentrations of customers, capital, and talent. If that pattern continues, digitalisation may raise national productivity while leaving the geography of economic value largely unchanged.
Asia-Pacific is already entering an extraordinary investment cycle. Cushman & Wakefield estimates that the region’s data-centre development pipeline reached 26.5GW in the first half of 2026. Johor alone has a pipeline of 3,088MW and approximately 1,110MW already operational. Bangkok’s pipeline reached 2,084MW, whilst Jakarta stood at 1,699MW. The obvious response is to build more. But scale alone is not a strategy.
Indonesia therefore needs to distinguish between comparative advantage and competitive advantage. Geography, market size, and natural resources are comparative advantages. Competitive advantage emerges only when those assets are integrated into an ecosystem that investors and networks find difficult to replace, including internet exchange, submarine cable, carrier-neutral data centre, cloud infrastructure, renewable power, satellite gateway, skilled talent, and commercial demand.
That changes how eastern Indonesia should be viewed. Jakarta has the country’s largest corporate and consumer demand base, whilst Batam is increasingly integrated with the Singapore-Johor ecosystem. But a strategy concentrated almost entirely around those corridors would leave Indonesia with a strong western interface and a comparatively weak eastern one. Indonesia’s geography offers another option: build a second digital corridor facing the Pacific.
Manado and Makassar should sit at the centre of that strategy, not because both should become large data-centre cities, but because they perform different functions. Manado has network geography. Makassar has economic gravity. The advantage emerges when both are integrated rather than duplicated.
Manado’s case became stronger with the landing of the Bifrost Cable System, which stretches for more than 20,000 kilometres and links Singapore and Indonesia with Davao, Guam, and the west coast of North America. This creates an eastbound trans-Pacific route that differs materially from Indonesia’s traditional dependence on western gateways.
That does not mean Manado should rush to build hyperscale capacity. Manado should therefore be measured not only by installed capacity, but by how many networks interconnect there, how much traffic can remain local, how much content can be cached closer to eastern Indonesian users, and whether it becomes a credible disaster-diversity route. A landing station creates limited value if traffic only passes through it. An interconnection ecosystem creates economic activity around that traffic.
Makassar provides the complementary side. It already serves as a major centre for trade, logistics, education, government, finance, and industry across eastern Indonesia. That gives it something Manado cannot easily reproduce: a broader and more immediate base of enterprise demand.
Its opportunity is therefore to become a regional compute and aggregation hub, where all generate workloads that do not inherently need to return to Jakarta. As cloud and AI adoption grows, more of that processing can occur closer to the source of economic activity.
The benefit is not simply lower latency. Compute infrastructure can create local demand for cloud engineers, cybersecurity specialists, disaster-recovery services, research capacity, and digital applications. This is how infrastructure can begin to influence the geography of GDP. It does not mechanically transfer output from Java to Sulawesi; it reduces structural disadvantages that have historically reinforced economic concentration.
That is why eastern digital infrastructure should be viewed as industrial policy, not telecommunications policy alone.
The regional environment strengthens this argument because the data-centre boom is increasingly constrained by electricity. Sulawesi has potentially useful fundamentals. PLN’s 2025-2034 electricity plan includes approximately 9,000 circuit-kilometres of new transmission infrastructure in Sulawesi, whilst around 7.7GW of additional renewable-energy capacity is planned for the island. This does not automatically make Sulawesi competitive for hyperscale computing, but it creates an opportunity to coordinate energy and digital infrastructure before investment decisions.
The same logic applies to resilience. Northern Sulawesi sits in an active seismic region. That should not weaken Manado’s case; it should shape the architecture. Manado can specialise in international interconnection and route diversity, whilst Makassar carries a larger share of regional compute and recovery capacity. The economic value of the second node lies precisely in the fact that it is not located in the same failure domain.
The objective is therefore not to shift digital activity away from Java. It is to use infrastructure to deepen regions that already have growth momentum. If computing, connectivity, energy, capital, and skills begin reinforcing one another, Sulawesi’s share of national output can rise because new value is being created there rather than simply relocated.
Indonesia does not need another data-centre boom for its own sake. It needs a more deliberate economic geography for the digital age. Jakarta and Batam can remain the western digital corridor, linked to Singapore and routes toward South Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. Makassar and Manado can form the foundations of an eastern corridor linking Indonesia’s domestic economy with Davao, Guam, and the Pacific, whilst terrestrial and satellite networks extend that corridor farther into eastern Indonesia.
Indonesia’s comparative advantage has always been visible on the map. Its competitive advantage will depend on whether it can turn that geography into an integrated system of connectivity, compute, energy, capital, talent, and business distribution.

articles.title: Consumer loan interest rates have risen sharply. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Consumer loan interest rates have risen sharply.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Interest rates on unsecured loans can reach 75% per year.
Mr. NS (Ho Chi Minh City) said he recently sold a house on Tran Xuan Soan Street (Tan Hung Ward) for 9 billion VND due to the pressure of high loan interest rates. He bought the house many years ago when interest rates were still low, but in recent months, interest rates have been steadily increasing, reaching 14-15% per year, forcing him to sell to pay off his debt. "Many of my friends borrowed even more, and when the preferential rates ended, they were charged a base interest rate of 13.5% plus a margin of 4-5%, bringing it up to 17.5-18.5% per year," Mr. NS said. On online forums over the past few days, many people have shared screenshots showing that interest rates for car loans ranging from 100 to 500 million VND have also risen to 19.5% per year.
Photo: Ngoc Thang
With domestic consumption increasingly expected to be a key driver of growth, a healthy consumer finance market will help connect people's needs with production, trade, and services.
Mr. Dao Minh Tu, Vice President and General Secretary of the Vietnam Banking Association
In fact, interest rates for home loans, car loans, consumer loans, etc., have increased in recent months compared to the end of last year as the base interest rate has risen. Techcombank announced its base/reference interest rate effective from September 15th, with unsecured consumer loans at 13%/year; and real estate loans, secured consumer loans, and car loans at 9%/year. By the end of September, Techcombank announced credit card interest rates ranging from 16% to 39.8%/year, specifically Techcombank Visa Standard at 39.8%/year, Techcombank Everyday at 38.88%/year, Techcombank Eco at 37.92%/year, and Techcombank Visa Infinite at 16%/year… In case the card balance becomes overdue, the overdue interest rate is 150% of the in-term interest rate. In addition, Techcombank's average lending interest rate disbursed in August was 11.2% per annum, with an average deposit-to-lending interest rate spread of 4.97% per annum.

Similarly, VPBank applies new interest rates to personal loans secured by collateral for real estate purchases and consumer purposes, ranging from 1 month to over 15 years. For loans with a 1-month adjustment period, the base interest rate is 11.3 - 13.3%/year; for loans with a 3-month adjustment period, the base interest rate is 12.1 - 13.8%/year. For loans to supplement working capital and car loans, the base interest rate ranges from 11.1 - 13.1%/year… Compared to the base interest rate announced at the end of 2025, this bank has increased it by 2.4 - 3%/year. AtACB , the base interest rate applied to loans with the term announced in October is 9.5%, an increase of 0.3% compared to the previous month.
A survey of consumer loan interest rates at financial companies shows high rates, especially for cash loans, reaching as high as 75% per year. At Home Credit Limited Liability Financial Company, the cash loan interest rate announced at the end of July was 45-55% for new customers, while existing customers had a minimum rate of 16.22% per year to a maximum of 49.5% per year. Loans for insurance premium payments, sold alongside the main loan, ranged from 16.2% to 55% per year. For credit cards, the installment conversion interest rate on the card balance ranged from 33.2% to 49.5% per year on a declining balance basis, depending on the credit assessment results of each cardholder at each time…
From October 1st, Mirae Asset Finance applies interest rates of 15-65% per year for cash loans to salaried employees, civil servants, teachers, and staff working at hospitals, clinics, schools, etc., for loan amounts from 5 to 500 million VND, with loan terms from 6 to 48 months. For quick consumer loans, customers with health insurance cards and female customers can borrow from 5 to 36 million VND at an interest rate of 55% per year. Loans based on credit card limits have interest rates from 52-58% per year. The highest interest rate offered by the company is 75% per year for unsecured cash loans, effective from September 22nd, while the lowest rate for this product is 35% per year. For installment purchase loans such as household goods, motorcycles, electric motorcycles, etc., interest rates range from 0 - 59% per year. The average lending interest rate as of the end of September for this unit was 43% per year for cash loans and 46.7% per year for installment purchase loans…
Consumer lending fuels shopping demand.
Financial expert, Dr. Nguyen Tri Hieu, analyzed that consumption accounts for a very large proportion of GDP, estimated at around 70-80%. Therefore, if we want to boost growth, we need solutions to support consumption, including creating conditions for people to access credit at reasonable costs. When interest rates on consumer loans are too high, people will limit borrowing and be more cautious in spending. This directly affects purchasing power, thereby impacting production, business activities, and GDP growth. Dr. Nguyen Tri Hieu commented that interest rates of around 30% per year for some consumer loans or credit card balances are already considered high, and rates exceeding 40% per year are extremely high.
According to Mr. Hieu, compared to corporate credit, consumer credit generally carries higher risks due to smaller loan sizes, diverse customer bases, and repayment ability heavily dependent on individual income and employment status. To compensate for this risk, banks and finance companies must factor the risk premium into lending interest rates. However, if consumer lending interest rates reach 30-40% or higher, two possibilities need to be considered. Firstly, credit risk in the economy is increasing. Secondly, financial institutions are applying excessively high interest rates compared to actual risk in order to increase profits.
"If borrowing costs are too high, people will reduce their need for borrowing and consumption. In the context of an economy aiming for high growth, towards 10% this year, excessively high consumer loan interest rates will be a significant obstacle. If purchasing power does not improve, achieving this growth target will face many challenges," warned Mr. Nguyen Tri Hieu.

At a recent meeting, Mr. Dao Minh Tu, Vice Chairman and General Secretary of the Vietnam Banking Association, noted that behind each loan lies a very specific need of a family: tuition fees that need to be paid on time, unexpected medical expenses, a vehicle for work, a household appliance that needs replacing, or essential expenses when income hasn't yet caught up. Looking more broadly, consumer finance is also significant for the functioning of the economy. When appropriate capital helps transform consumer demand into actual purchasing power, goods and services circulate better, businesses have more outlets, and production and business activities are supported. "In the context of domestic consumption increasingly expected to be an important driver of growth, a healthy consumer finance market will contribute to connecting people's needs with production, trade, and service activities," Mr. Dao Minh Tu emphasized.
Outstanding consumer credit and card debt is approximately 4.62 trillion VND.
According to the Vietnam Banking Association, by the end of August 2026, outstanding loans for living expenses and credit card balances across the entire banking system reached approximately VND 4.62 trillion, an increase of 21.75% compared to the same period last year and accounting for 22.56% of the total outstanding credit balance in the economy. This scale shows that consumer finance has become a significant part of credit activities, directly linked to people's purchasing power and the circulation of goods and services.
